paragraphs: Good first try if: you are willing to focus for long periods on listening and transcribing while sitting at a workstation operating stenographic equipment, can record word for word according to format, proofread spelling and punctuation accurately, and stay steady under the strict accuracy demands of court hearings and meetings.

Think carefully: if you cannot tolerate long periods of sitting and high-intensity repetitive hand motions, or the strict requirements for word-for-word accuracy and the seriousness of the consequences, the actual work will not match your expectations.

The core output is accurate, checkable verbatim records and written transcripts: dictation without error, accurate symbol-to-text conversion, complete proofreading, clear filing and exhibit registration, and anomalies handled according to procedure, not 'typing fast' or 'plenty of experience'.

Low-risk check: complete one 'listen and record — convert to text — proofread — file' exercise using fictional materials; it only judges work preferences, does not touch real hearings or party data, and is not equivalent to an occupational qualification or a hiring outcome.

Decision center: whether, under strict accuracy and serious-consequence requirements, you can make verbatim recording, proofreading and verification, and filing and archiving traceable and within authority.

Work rhythm is set by hearing and meeting schedules and transcription and proofreading deadlines; court hearings, legislative meetings, depositions and real-time captioning differ markedly in their subject matter, timeliness and accuracy requirements.

Similar job titles do not mean the same duties; when comparing, first look at whether the object is verbatim recording and transcription, legal document assistance, court documents and licensing, data entry or general administration, and whether it carries word-for-word accuracy and consequence responsibility.

Stenographic equipment, computer-aided transcription and speech recognition may be treated as controlled aids, but automatic recognition results or symbol conversion must not be treated as a final record that has not been manually proofread, nor may system output be treated as the final basis for filing, archiving or verification.
The fit judgment should be based on real hearing or meeting shadowing, rework feedback and unit process checks, and is not replaced by an interest type or a single test.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional materials; party information, exhibits and records in real hearings and meetings must be handled according to the process and applicable rules of the unit where you work.

Where is the boundary between court reporters and real-time captioners and the adjacent legal, clerical and transcription posts?

Compare verbatim recording, legal assistance, court municipal licensing, office clerical work, data entry and medical records by actual duty; adjacent posts are not all in legal settings, court clerk Core includes transcribing dictation and word processing Core includes recording and dictation input, so they cannot be absolutely excluded on the basis of whether they take dictation.
Core purpose

Turn the spoken word in hearings, meetings and events into a checkable verbatim written record, ensuring accurate dictation, complete transcription, proper proofreading and verification, and traceable filing and archiving.

Core purposes of adjacent roles: paralegals prepare legal documents and assist with cases; court, municipal and licensing clerks handle court documents and licensing; office clerks handle general administration and clerical work; data entry keyers enter data in batches; word processors and typists enter and format documents; medical records specialists manage medical records and coding.
Main object and basis
The spoken content, procedure and exhibits of hearings and meetings; the basis is law and court procedure, record and transcription format standards, and confidentiality and records rules.

Objects and bases of adjacent roles: cases and legal documents (paralegals), court documents and licensing (court clerks), general documents and administration (office clerks), data and forms (data entry keyers), documents and format (word processors), medical records and coding (medical records specialists).
Core process
Real-time verbatim recording → ask the speaker to clarify → convert symbols to text → transcribe and proofread → verify → file and archive and provide records.

Processes of adjacent roles: document preparation and case assistance (paralegals), document checking and permit intake (court clerks), document handling and archiving (office clerks), batch entry and verification (data entry keyers), entry and formatting (word processors), record organizing and coding (medical records specialists).
Main output
Accurate verbatim written records, checkable proofs, and complete filing and exhibit registration.

Outputs of adjacent roles: legal documents and case materials (paralegals), court document and permit records (court clerks), documents and archives (office clerks), entered data (data entry keyers), finished documents (word processors), medical records and coding (medical records specialists).
Responsible party

Court reporters and real-time captioners are responsible for the accuracy of verbatim recording and transcription, proofreading and verification, the traceability of filing and exhibit registration, and confidentiality; legal judgment and rulings are not decided by them.

Responsible parties of adjacent roles: paralegals are responsible for document preparation; court clerks for document and permit compliance; office clerks for the accuracy of documents and archives; data entry keyers for entry accuracy; word processors for finished documents; medical records specialists for the accuracy of records and coding.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with judges and court staff, lawyers and parties, and meeting organizers according to process; when a passage is unclear, a record is disputed, an exhibit problem arises, a disclosure request arises, or a matter exceeds authorization, escalate according to procedure and keep records; when training new colleagues, demonstrate according to process.

Collaboration of adjacent roles: paralegals with lawyers and parties; court clerks with judges and the public; office clerks with all departments; data entry keyers with business departments; word processors with document requesters; medical records specialists with clinicians and the coding department.
Boundary of conclusions

Compare the main task purposes and the actual jurisdiction duties; a name or adjacency does not grant authority, and other clerical posts also have proofreading or transcription tasks, so word-for-word accuracy responsibility cannot be written as unique to this occupation.

The preparation levels and employment conditions of adjacent roles do not apply to this occupation and must be checked item by item against each occupation's official materials and the rules of the unit where you work.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether the dictation is verbatim and accurate; whether unclear passages are clarified with the speaker and marked; whether symbol-to-text conversion and the transcription format are correct; whether spelling and punctuation proofreading is thorough; whether record verification and filing and archiving are complete; and whether record disputes or beyond-authorization matters are escalated according to procedure.

Record completely and clarify according to the real record standards, and avoid conjecture and summarization; errors may trigger checking and disputes, and the specific evidentiary effect is judged according to jurisdiction and the facts, so it is not claimed that any rewriting automatically loses evidentiary value.
Editorial risk analysis: when a statement is unclear, ask the speaker to clarify or clearly mark it as to be verified; filling in by guesswork may make the record inconsistent with the facts.

Editorial risk analysis: convert stenographic symbols to text correctly and transcribe according to the established format; conversion or format errors may make the written record unusable or require rework.

Checking spelling, proper nouns and numbers are task leads; punctuation and the specific finalization rules are checked against the actual system, and the effect of errors on the admissibility of evidence is checked separately.

Editorial risk analysis: verify accuracy against the source record, register and keep exhibits, and file and archive a readable written record; missing verification or archiving may make the record harder to trace.
Judgment five: are record verification and filing complete?

values: Fictional dictation and captioning scenario materials (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: a reporter faces four problems during a day of hearings and one meeting captioning assignment. First, a speaker talks quickly with an accent and some words are unclear; second, a statement involving an amount figure shows uncertainty in the number when converted to text; third, an exhibit was returned without being registered with a number; fourth, a lawyer asks for a written record the same day, but proofreading is not finished.

Materials provided: the dictation marking standards; the transcription format and glossary; the exhibit registration and filing process; the proofreading checklist; the rules for providing written records and confidentiality.

Materials not provided: the criteria for judging whether to interrupt to clarify an unclear passage, the verification authority when a number is uncertain, and the approval authority for providing a record before proofreading has been completed. If the exercise requires these conditions, write out your assumptions and the party to be consulted explicitly.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and handover plan, including the arrangement for marking and clarifying unclear passages, the way to verify and annotate an uncertain number, the handling and supplementary registration of an unregistered exhibit, and the handling and handover items when a record whose proofreading is not finished is requested in advance.

The plan should state which information comes from the exercise materials and which is still an assumption, and explain whether the basis is the marking standards, the format and glossary or the filing process.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the exercise)

The plan should include: unclear passages (mark them as to be verified according to the standards, ask the speaker to clarify or play back according to procedure, and do not fill in by guesswork), numbers (check the source audio and context, annotate the uncertainty and confirm it through the glossary and verification process, and do not decide on your own), exhibits (pause the return, supplement the registration number according to procedure and record the handler and time, without altering the original registration), advance provision (explain that proofreading is not finished, consult according to procedure, provide within what authorization and confidentiality allow and mark it as to be verified, and do not deliver an unfinalized draft on your own), and handover (state clearly the status of the four items, the actions taken and the items still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the basis for judgment is enough.

Real unit, hearing or party information must not be used; when real records, exhibits and authority are involved, the rules of the unit where you work must be followed.

entries.answer: Use a stenograph, electronic stenographic equipment or computer recording equipment to record hearings, legislative sessions, committee meetings and depositions verbatim in real time, convert stenographic symbols to text and display them, ask the speaker to clarify unclear statements, transcribe according to the established format and proofread spelling and punctuation, verify record accuracy and check with the judge, provide written records on request, file readable written records with the clerk of court's office, register, keep and archive exhibits, administer oaths to witnesses, read back recorded portions in court, and provide real-time captioning for meetings or events and transmit real-time text streams to judges and lawyers.
entries.question: What do court reporters and real-time captioners actually do every day?

entries.answer: Court reporters and real-time captioners record and transcribe spoken content verbatim and carry word-for-word accuracy responsibility; paralegals and legal assistants prepare legal documents and assist with cases under the direction of a lawyer; court, municipal and licensing clerks handle court documents and licensing and usually do not take verbatim dictation; data entry keyers enter existing data in batches; word processors and typists enter and format documents; medical records specialists manage medical records and coding.
entries.question: What is the difference between court reporters and real-time captioners and paralegals or court clerks?

entries.answer: Speech recognition and automatic transcription, computer-aided transcription, real-time captioning tools and cloud computing can reduce manual symbol conversion, draft transcription and some caption generation; but word-for-word accuracy in live dictation, clarifying unclear passages, proofreading proper nouns and numbers, verifying against the source record, filing and exhibit management, and reading back in court still depend on people and are bound by law and institutional rules. Technical exposure does not equal organizational adoption or job disappearance.
entries.question: How will AI affect or replace court reporters and real-time captioners?

entries.answer: What can be verified is change at the task level: three types of task — symbol-to-text and draft transcription, real-time caption generation, and filing and retrieval — can be partly taken on by tools; this page has no single-occupation adoption or replacement data.
entries.question: Which tasks of court reporters and real-time captioners already have evidence of AI-driven change?

entries.answer: Verbatim dictation and clarifying unclear passages, proofreading proper nouns and numbers, transcription format and verification, filing and exhibit management, immediate correction of real-time captions, and the awareness of review and confidentiality when using systems.
entries.question: Facing AI, which abilities should court reporters and real-time captioners still focus on validating?

description.text: Court Reporters and Simultaneous Captioners (O*NET-SOC 27-3092.00) turn the spoken word in hearings, meetings and events into a checkable verbatim written record: this covers real-time recording with a stenograph or computer, symbol-to-text conversion, asking the speaker to clarify, transcription and proofreading according to format, providing written records on request, filing and archiving records and exhibits, verifying accuracy, reading back in court and administering oaths to witnesses, and real-time captioning and live streams; it includes the US 2025 median annual wage of 72,420 USD (hourly wage 34.82 USD), about 17,700 people employed in 2024, little or no change in the 2024—2034 employment projection, the gap in mainland Chinese occupation-level wages and employment basis, and control points for highly repetitive operations, accuracy consequences and deadline pressure.

subject.name: Court reporters and real-time captioners
subject.summary: Court Reporters and Simultaneous Captioners corresponds in the US to O*NET-SOC 27-3092.00 (Court Reporters and Simultaneous Captioners). The core is turning spoken language and proceedings verbatim into a checkable written record: recording the verbatim content of hearings, legislative sessions and committee proceedings in real time with a stenograph or computer recording equipment, converting stenographic symbols to text and displaying them, asking the speaker to clarify unclear statements when necessary, transcribing according to the established format and proofreading spelling, providing written records to judges, lawyers or the public, filing and archiving records and registering and keeping exhibits, verifying the accuracy of records and rulings, reading back recorded portions on request in court and administering oaths to witnesses, and providing real-time captioning for meetings and events and transmitting real-time text streams to judges and lawyers. On the Chinese side, comparable posts are mostly court stenographers, meeting stenographers and captioners, are not one-to-one with this US occupation breakdown, and their employment and pay bases cannot be interchanged.
